newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli bonds end little changed in quiet trade.
newsitem.headline: Israeli bonds end little changed in quiet trade.

text.p: Israeli bonds closed little changed on Thursday with the market waiting for the July consumer price index (CPI), traders said.
Indices:
* Government bonds general: -0.04 pct to 110.10
* CPI-linked government bonds: -0.03 pct to 110.16
* Unlinked government bonds: unchanged at 109.93
* Dollar-linked government bonds: -0.22 pct to 110.00
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.03 pct to 108.05
Volume including Makams was a low 121 million shekels.
"Trading was quiet today. The market is stable at these levels, with most bonds unchanged. Basically the market is waiting to see what July's CPI will be," Ilan Doron of Solid Financial Markets said.
July's CPI will be released on August 15.
"The coming CPI is crucial and no one knows what it will be. At the moment it appears that the dollar won't have as much effect on inflation as it had in the previous month," Doron said.

The rise of the dollar against the shekel in June, which caused June's CPI to rise 1.1 percent, had triggered fears of a series of high indices. The shekel has recovered some of its losses against the dollar in the past two weeks.
The shekel weakened against the dollar on Thursday. The representative rate for the dollar was fixed at 3.5220 shekels compared with 3.5140 on Wednesday.
Yields of one-year unlinked bonds were stable at 13 percent on Thursday, while yields of CPI-linked long bonds were stable at around 3.9 percent, Doron said.
"Traders are waiting to see where the market is going," said Ofer Dori at Ofek Securities.
Dori added that the market was not expecting a change in interest rates on July 28.

The Bank of Israel slashed its base lending rate in mid-June by 1.2 percentage points to an annualised 12.7 percent. The central bank will announce its monthly monetary programme for August on July 28, at the monthly review.
Prices of dollar-linked bonds closed lower on Thursday despite a weakening of the shekel against the dollar, Dori said.
Doron said that the government's decision to further cut the 1997 budget had not really affected the market. "The amount is not so significant and I don't see it affecting the bond market," he said.
The Israeli cabinet approved an 800 million shekel cut in the 1997 budget.
The cuts were the third round of budget contraction since the draft 1997 budget was presented last autumn.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
($1 = 3.52 shekels)
